neighbours.label: Animal sensory organs and specialised senses in natural-history/biology prose (electroreceptors, magnetoreception, lateral line, compound eyes, echolocation, heat pits); peaks on the sense-organ word. Weaker for non-sensory body anatomy (keratin, claws) and for smell via antennae; also fires on 'Journal of Comparative Physiology'
fire: Sharks can sense the faint electric pulses of a buried flounder through pores on their snouts.
Many birds carry receptors that let them read Earth's magnetic field during migration.
A blind cave fish relies on its lateral line to feel the movement of water around rocks.
Dragonflies scan for prey with huge compound eyes made of nearly thirty thousand facets.
Horseshoe bats emit ultrasonic calls and build a picture of the moth from the returning echoes.
Boas and pythons detect infrared heat from warm-blooded prey through pits along their lips.
Owls have asymmetric ear openings so they can pinpoint a mouse's rustle in the dark.
Honeybees see ultraviolet patterns on petals that are invisible to the human eye.
quiet: Sharks can go for weeks without eating after a large meal of seal.
Many birds fly south in large flocks during the autumn migration.
A blind cave fish lives its whole life in dark underground pools in Mexico.
Dragonflies spend most of their lives as larvae living underwater in ponds.
Horseshoe bats hibernate in old mines and caves through the winter months.
Boas and pythons swallow their prey whole and digest it over several days.
Owls lay their eggs in old tree hollows and barn lofts.
Honeybees have a barbed stinger that tears away from the body after they sting.

predictions: 8/8 fire above 0.20; near misses low, the bee stinger (non-sensory anatomy) is the riskiest
